strengths: Insightful analysis of the 'detection-association conflict' in MOTR, demonstrating that MOTR-like models inherently possess strong, under-utilized detection capabilities when evaluated without active track queries.
Systematic and clear exploration of four alternative strategies for injecting detection priors, which serves as a valuable design reference for the tracking community.

The proposed SelfMOTR is elegant and self-contained, avoiding heavy external detectors (unlike MOTRv2) or complex query-management systems, thereby preserving the end-to-end purity of query-based trackers.

Strong experimental performance on DanceTrack, outperforming the MOTR baseline by a large margin (HOTA 51.2 -> 69.2) and achieving highly competitive state-of-the-art results with exceptional association accuracy (AssA 59.3).
Thorough ablations, including speed/efficiency profiling (showing 20.7 FPS on a Tesla L40S) and structural variations (e.g., varying decoder depth for the self-proposal pass).
weaknesses: Computational overhead of the dual-pass decoder architecture: although the heavy backbone encoder is run only once, the decoder must be run twice per frame, which reduces overall throughput (FPS drops from 24.8 to 20.7).

On MOT17, the performance of SelfMOTR (57.5 HOTA) does not show an improvement over the MOTR baseline (57.8 HOTA), suggesting that the self-proposal mechanism is less robust in highly crowded street scenes where external detectors typically dominate.

Additional hyperparameter dependency: the introduction of proposal thresholds ($c_{prop}$), the number of extra learned proposal anchors, and loss weighting coefficients adds to the model's overall tuning complexity.

strengths: The paper provides an interesting and thorough empirical analysis demonstrating that MOTR-style trackers possess strong latent detection capability which is suppressed when track queries are enabled.
The systematic comparison of four different strategies for injecting detection priors (pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, and anchor proposals) is highly insightful and well-structured.

SelfMOTR successfully avoids dependency on external detectors (e.g., YOLOX used in MOTRv2/v3), maintaining a fully self-contained, detector-free, and end-to-end pipeline while achieving strong association accuracy.
The model demonstrates competitive tracking performance on DanceTrack, achieving 69.2 HOTA and the highest association score (59.3 AssA) among compared end-to-end methods.
The dual-pass design is optimized computationally by executing the heavy encoder only once, resulting in a minor speed penalty (from 24.8 FPS to 20.7 FPS on a Tesla L40S).
weaknesses: On the MOT17 dataset (Table 4), SelfMOTR's performance (57.5 HOTA) is slightly inferior to the baseline MOTR (57.8 HOTA) and behind other end-to-end methods like CO-MOT (60.1 HOTA). The reason for this degradation on MOT17 is not fully resolved.
While running the decoder twice is computationally managed, it still introduces a 17% speed reduction compared to standard MOTR, which may be a drawback for high-throughput applications.

The dual-pass formulation adds some implementation complexity (e.g., thresholding, concatenation, and dual losses) compared to the simple, unified single-pass design of original end-to-end tracking transformers.

The proposed self-proposal mechanism is only evaluated on the MOTR baseline; its generalizability and compatibility with more advanced query-based tracking architectures (like CO-MOT or MOTRv3) remain unexplored in the experiments.

strengths: Insightful analysis of the detection-association conflict: The paper starts with a key empirical observation that MOTR-like models exhibit substantially better detection performance when track queries are removed during inference. This observation is simple yet highly motivating.

Systematic evaluation of prior-injection mechanisms: The authors conduct a structured study of four different strategies (pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, and anchor proposals) to identify the most effective way to utilize detection priors, which serves as a valuable guide for future research.

Detector-free end-to-end design: Unlike MOTRv2/v3, which rely on heavy external detectors (like YOLOX), SelfMOTR generates its own proposals internally via a dual-pass mechanism with shared weights. This successfully preserves the self-contained, end-to-end elegance of tracking transformers.

Strong performance on DanceTrack: On the DanceTrack dataset, SelfMOTR achieves highly competitive performance (69.2 HOTA, 72.5 IDF1) and achieves the highest association accuracy (59.3 AssA) among the compared end-to-end methods, demonstrating the benefit of better feature alignment.

Efficiency: By running the heavy backbone encoder only once per frame and utilizing a shallow proposal-generation pass, SelfMOTR only incurs a minor speed penalty (20.7 FPS vs. 24.8 FPS for baseline MOTR on a Tesla L40S GPU).
weaknesses: Performance regression on MOT17: In Table 4, on the MOT17 test set, SelfMOTR achieves 57.5 HOTA, which is slightly lower than the baseline MOTR (57.8 HOTA), as well as other end-to-end models like CO-MOT (60.1 HOTA) and MOTRv3 (60.2 HOTA). It remains unclear why the self-proposal mechanism leads to significant gains on DanceTrack but a slight regression on MOT17.

Conceptual novelty: The idea of utilizing a dual-pass decoder or generating candidate proposals internally shares conceptual similarities with previous cascade query frameworks or methods like CO-MOT (which uses auxiliary shadow queries). The distinction between the proposed dual-pass paradigm and traditional two-stage/cascade query decoding is somewhat incremental.

Missing ablation on hyper-parameters of proposals: The paper lacks detailed analysis on how the number of generated proposals ($N_{prop}$) and the number of learned proposal anchors ($N_{learned} = 10$) affect tracking performance across different scenarios (e.g., highly crowded vs. sparse frames).

strengths: The paper introduces an elegant, detector-free dual-pass decoding framework (SelfMOTR) that effectively leverages the model's latent detection capacity, resolving the detection-association conflict without external detectors.
The analysis using 'Track Attention Mass' and attention entropy to diagnose query interference is highly insightful, drawing neat parallels to attention sink phenomena in LLMs.
The ablation studies are exceptionally thorough, step-by-step evaluating various prior injection strategies (pretraining, distillation, anchors) to justify the final architecture.
The proposed method achieves strong performance on challenging datasets with complex/non-linear motions (DanceTrack, BFT, AnimalTrack) while remaining computationally efficient (20.7 FPS).
weaknesses: On the standard MOT17 dataset, the method's performance (58.4 HOTA) lags behind some existing end-to-end and non-end-to-end trackers, showing that the dual-pass proposal mechanism might have limited benefits when tracking under stable camera and pedestrian movement.
Although a shallow decoder can be used for the first pass, executing the decoder twice still introduces additional computational complexity and latency compared to a single-pass MOTR.

strengths: The paper provides a deeply insightful diagnostic analysis of query interference in joint-decoding transformer trackers. The introduction of 'Track Attention Mass' and Shannon entropy to analyze attention dynamics successfully explains why joint detection-association models suffer from detection degradation.

The proposed SelfMOTR is elegant and conceptually clean. By leveraging the model's own detection-only mode to generate native spatial proposals internally, it solves the detection-association conflict without relying on external pre-trained detectors, thereby maintaining a truly self-contained, end-to-end architecture.

The experimental validation is solid. The method achieves very strong, competitive results on highly dynamic datasets such as DanceTrack (69.2 HOTA, leading association score of 59.3 AssA) and sets new state-of-the-art results for end-to-end trackers on Bird Flock Tracking (BFT) and AnimalTrack.

The paper is very well-structured and includes comprehensive ablation studies that systematically justify each design choice, comparing different ways of injecting priors (e.g., query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposal).
weaknesses: Computational overhead: Running a dual-pass decoder (once for proposal generation, once for tracking) leads to a decline in inference speed from 24.8 FPS to 20.7 FPS (a ~16% speed drop). While the authors show that a shallow decoder can mitigate this, the dual-pass execution remains a drawback for real-time deployment.

Performance on static/pedestrian scenes (MOT17): As shown in Table 5, the performance of SelfMOTR on the MOT17 dataset still lags behind other end-to-end methods such as MOTRv3 and CO-MOT, and falls significantly short of non-end-to-end approaches. This shows that the internal proposal generator is less competitive in scenarios where standard high-quality detectors excel.
Lack of detailed parameter and GFLOPs comparisons against prior works (like MOTRv2/v3 or CO-MOT) to fully contextualize the trade-off of the dual-pass architecture.

Minor formatting and polishing issues: The paper contains several placeholders and unfinished headers, such as 'Abbreviated paper title' and 'F. Author et al.' on headers, and an empty 'Project page:' URL in the abstract.

strengths: Decouples proposal generation from association without requiring external detectors (like YOLOX in MOTRv2/v3), maintaining a fully end-to-end, unified tracker.
Provides a detailed diagnostic analysis using a newly defined 'Track-Attention Mass', borrowing insights from attention sinks in LLMs to explain the joint-decoding bottleneck and query interference.
Thoroughly investigates and compares four different strategies for injecting detection priors (Table 1), providing valuable insights for future query-based tracking research.
Achieves strong performance on DanceTrack (69.2 HOTA), and state-of-the-art results among end-to-end models on Bird Flock Tracking (71.1 HOTA) and AnimalTrack (45.5 HOTA).
weaknesses: Computational overhead of the dual-pass decoder: Running the transformer decoder twice per frame increases the inference cost and lowers the processing speed (from 24.8 to 20.7 FPS).

On the DanceTrack dataset, the overall HOTA (69.2) and detection accuracy (80.9 DetA) are slightly below CO-MOT (69.4 HOTA, 82.1 DetA), showing that the self-proposal pass does not fully resolve the detection gap compared to shadow-query-based methods.

The performance on the MOT17 dataset (Table 5 in the Appendix) is relatively weak compared to MOTRv3 and CO-MOT, indicating that the dual-pass strategy may struggle in crowded static scenes where precise detection localization is highly critical.

Lacks clarity on the exact default configuration of the decoder layers used in the proposal-generation pass for the main results (Tables 2, 3)—specifically, whether a full 6-layer pass or a truncated pass was utilized.
